s.877.8 seconds in a bottle, 887.7 in a be: In a bottle, neutrons last 877.8 seconds. In a beam, 887.7 seconds. That is ten seconds apart, about four standard deviations. A 2024 beam experiment at J-PARC counted electrons instead of protons. It agrees with the bottles. So the suspect is the proton-counting beams.
s.<b>Helium:</b> no dark line. Its stronge: Helium: no dark line. Its strongest yellow line, D3 at 587.7 nm, sits right next to sodium's pair. But the Sun's surface is too cool to take it out of the light. Helium was first seen in 1868, as a bright line in the Sun during an eclipse. That was 27 years before anyone found it on Earth. It is named for the Sun (helios).
s.<b>New in 2026:</b> clocks that tick on: New in 2026: clocks that tick on a change inside a nucleus. A laser first excited thorium-229 in 2024. In October 2026, two groups reported working nuclear clocks.
s.<b>{El}:</b> none of its lines land on t: {El}: none of its lines land on the Sun's dark lines. That does not prove it is absent. It may just be too rare, or too cool here, to leave a mark.
s.<b>{El}:</b> {n, plural, one {# peak} ot: {El}: {n, plural, one {# peak} other {# peaks}}, one for each subshell. The peak farthest to the left is {name}, at about {top} MJ/mol ({top2} eV). {count, plural, one {Its # electron sits} other {Its # electrons sit}} closest to the nucleus. The easiest to remove is {name2}, at about {last} MJ/mol (measured: {meas} MJ/mol). A peak's height is how many electrons share that energy. Its position is how tightly they are held.

{El}: {n, plural, one {# peak} other {# peaks}}, one for each subshell. The peak farthest to the left is {name}, at about {top} MJ/mol ({top2} eV). {count, plural, one {Its # electron sits} other {Its # electrons sit}} closest to the nucleus. The easiest to remove is {name2}, at about {last} MJ/mol. A peak's height is how many electrons share that energy. Its position is how tightly they are held.
s.<b>σ = 0.90 GeV/fm</b>, the string tensi: σ = 0.90 GeV/fm is the string tension. One GeV per femtometer is 1.602 × 10⁵ newtons, about 16.3 metric tons of force. So this string pulls with 14.7 metric tons, no matter how long it is. Lmin is the total length of the three legs. They meet at a point where every angle is 120°. A = 0.137 is the short-range part, which works like an electric pull.
s.A <b>proton</b> is two up quarks and one: A proton is two up quarks and one down quark (uud). A neutron is one up and two down (udd). An up quark carries +⅔ charge. A down quark carries −⅓. Add them: a proton is +1, a neutron is 0. That is where charge comes from.
s.A block is named for the subshell being: A block is named for the subshell that fills up across that part of the table. {El}'s configuration is {cfg}. So it sits in the {bk}-block.
s.A lone proton has nothing to bind to, so: A lone proton has nothing to hold on to. Its real binding energy is 0. The formula is made for nuclei with many particles, so it means nothing here.
s.A single p or d orbital is lobed and dir: One p or d orbital has lobes that point in a direction. But add up all the orbitals in a full subshell and the lobes cancel. The total is perfectly round (Unsöld's theorem). Switch on All shells and a noble gas comes out as a sphere.
s.Abundance doesn't follow the rows. Four: Abundance does not follow the rows. Four elements make up most of the crust: oxygen, silicon, aluminum, and iron. Rocks sort elements by their chemistry. Across the lanthanides you can see the Oddo–Harkins rule: elements with an even atomic number are more common than their odd neighbors. So cerium beats praseodymium, and neodymium beats both of its neighbors.
s.Across a row it climbs, from an alkali m: Across a row it climbs. An alkali metal gives up its one outer electron easily. A noble gas holds on hard. The small dips are real. Where a new p subshell starts (boron, aluminum, gallium), the first p electron is easier to remove. Where a p orbital first holds two electrons (oxygen, sulfur, selenium), they push on each other, so one is easier to remove. The biggest drops inside a row come right after a d subshell fills: zinc to gallium, cadmium to indium, and mercury to thallium. The last one is the largest.
s.Add two neutrons to make carbon-14. Cosm: Add two neutrons to make carbon-14. Cosmic rays make it in the air. It decays at a steady rate, and that is the clock that dates wood and bone.
s.Add up the three quark masses and you ge: Add up the three quark masses and you get about 1% of the proton's mass. The other 99% is pure energy: the gluon field, and the quarks moving around inside. Nearly all the mass of everything you touch is binding energy, not stuff.
s.Almost all the mass of the atom is in a: Almost all the mass of the atom is in a tiny speck at the middle. It is tens of thousands of times smaller than the cloud. Zoom in (scroll, or click the orange dot) until it turns into balls.
s.Amber balls are <b>protons</b> (positive: Amber balls are protons (positive charge). Slate balls are neutrons (no charge). Together they are called nucleons. The number of protons is Z. It decides which element this is. The total number of nucleons is A.
s.An electron has no orbit and no crisp ed: An electron has no orbit and no sharp edge. Each dot is one place the electron could be. The dots are drawn at random, with the right odds. Pile up enough dots and the shape of the odds appears. More dots means more likely.
s.An orbital is not an orbit. It is the sh: An orbital is not an orbit. It is the shape of the electron's wave, |ψ|². It says where the electron is likely to be found. The electron has no path. A measurement finds it somewhere in that cloud. A charge going in circles would give off light and spiral into the nucleus in less than a billionth of a second (The math, step 3).
s.Approximate shares of the Solar System&r: Rough shares of the Solar System's supply, after Johnson (2019). Merging neutron stars stand in for all rapid neutron capture. Rare supernovae may make some of it.
s.Beryllium-8 splits into two helium-4 nuc: Beryllium-8 splits into two helium-4 nuclei in about 10⁻¹⁶ seconds. Stars get past this by catching a third helium nucleus before it splits. That is how the universe makes its carbon.
s.Binding energy is energy that left when: Binding energy is energy that left when the nucleus formed. So the nucleus weighs less than its parts, by B/c²: {B} MeV ÷ 931.5 MeV per u = {B2} u missing. A reactor or a star gives that missing mass back as energy.
s.Binding energy per nucleon, in MeV, agai: Binding energy per nucleon, in MeV, against the number of nucleons. The dots are measured masses. The line is the liquid-drop formula above. The white dot is iron.
s.Bohr's rule gets one-electron atoms righ: Bohr's rule works for atoms with one electron. It fails for everything else. And it cannot say why the rule holds. Step 5 gives the reason. Step 7 deals with many electrons.
s.Chlorine pulls the shared pair toward it: Chlorine pulls the shared pair of electrons toward itself. So the molecule has a negative end and a positive end. Dissolved in water it is hydrochloric acid, the acid in your stomach.
s.Density depends on how atoms pack in a s: Density depends on how heavy the atoms are, and on how they pack in a solid. It peaks in the middle of each row: boron and aluminum in the short rows, the transition metals in the long ones. It drops to the gases at the end. Osmium and iridium are the densest ever measured. The row 7 values are predictions.
s.Down a column abundance mostly falls pas: Down a column, abundance mostly falls past row 3. Heavier nuclei are harder for stars to make. Row 2 is the exception. Lithium, beryllium, and boron are rare because stars destroy them. So sodium, magnesium, and aluminum are far more common.
s.Down a column it rises only a little: th: Down a column it rises only a little. The extra protons are mostly hidden by the extra inner shells. The outer electron is farther away, so it is usually held less tightly.
s.Down a column of the main groups atoms g: Down a column of the main groups, atoms grow. Every row adds a shell of electrons. After the lanthanides they barely grow at all. Hafnium is no bigger than zirconium. This is called the lanthanide contraction.
s.Down a column of the main groups it fall: Down a column of the main groups it falls. Each step adds a shell. So the outer electrons sit farther from the nucleus, behind more inner electrons. Among the heavy transition metals it often rises instead. Gold is more electronegative than copper. The 4f electrons shield poorly, so they let the nucleus pull the outer electrons in. This is the lanthanide contraction.

Down a column of the main groups it falls. The outer electron is more shells out, so it is easier to pull away. That is why cesium reacts more violently than lithium. In the heavy transition metals it can rise instead. Gold holds on tighter than silver.
Down a column the trend can go either way. The alkali metals melt more easily as they get bigger. So does carbon's group, from carbon down to tin. Lead melts a little higher than tin. The halogens go the other way. Fluorine melts at −220 °C and iodine at 114 °C, because bigger molecules attract each other more.
s.Drop hydrogen&rsquo;s electron from leve: Drop hydrogen’s electron from level 3 to level 2. The energy leaves as one photon of red light. For a one-electron atom that is the Rydberg formula. Every line below is computed from it:
s.Each square is one nucleus: a number of: Each square is one nucleus: a number of protons and a number of neutrons. Stable nuclei, and the isotopes Atom lists, are measured. The rest of the map is the liquid-drop model's estimate. It says where nuclei stop holding together, and which way they decay. It is rough at the edges.
s.Electronegativity: Pauling scale. Energy: Electronegativity: the Pauling scale. Energy to remove an electron: the first ionization energy, from the NIST Atomic Spectra Database. Pull on the outer electron: Slater's estimate of the charge it feels.
s.Elements 119 and 120 would begin a new r: Elements 119 and 120 would start a new row of the table. Nobody has made either one yet. Whether the heaviest nuclei have an island of stability is still an open question.
s.Elements are laid out by proton count <s: Elements are laid out by proton count, Z: left to right, top to bottom. Each step adds one proton and one electron. The table is really a map of how electrons fill up.
s.Elements in a column have the same outer: Elements in a column have the same pattern of outer electrons. So they behave alike. The left column is metals that react violently. The right column is noble gases that barely react at all. Chemistry rhymes down a column.
s.Every element glows in its own set of co: Every element glows in its own set of colors. Atom does not carry {el}’s measured lines yet. So here is hydrogen, the one atom whose spectrum is exact arithmetic.
s.Every occupied orbital at once, 60,000 M: Every occupied orbital at once, from 60,000 random samples. Brightness is on a log scale. The K shell is ten thousand times denser than the outer shell. Click the orange dot to fall into the nucleus.
s.Every radio antenna works because accele: Every radio antenna works because moving charges give off waves when they speed up or turn. An orbiting electron turns all the time. It would give off light, lose energy, and spiral into the nucleus. Work out how fast, and atoms would not last the blink of an eye. They last billions of years. So something in classical physics has to give.
s.Everything you have ever touched is some: Everything you have ever touched is some number of these three particles. Protons decide the element. Neutrons decide whether it lasts. Electrons decide how it bonds.
s.Fall into <span data-el=\"lname\">iron</: Fall into iron one scroll at a time. See its electron cloud, the light it gives off, the empty space inside it, its nucleus, a proton, and the quarks you can try to pull out. Every picture is computed live.
s.Fall into silicon's electron cloud. It h: Fall into silicon's electron cloud. It has four outer electrons. Add a trace of an element with three or five, and it becomes a conductor that a voltage can switch on and off.
s.For each size there is an ideal proton-t: For each size there is a best mix of protons and neutrons. That is the valley of stability. Stray from it and the nucleus decays (beta or alpha) to climb back down. The N–Z map and the decay chains on the Nucleus tab show this.
s.Four bonds and no lone pairs: the four g: Four bonds and no lone pairs. The four groups sit as far apart as they can, at the corners of a tetrahedron, 109.5° apart. The C–H pulls are small and point every way, so they cancel.
s.Gluons have no mass at all. About 99 per: Gluons have no mass at all. About 99 percent of a proton's mass is energy. The quarks move at nearly the speed of light inside a femtometer, and the gluon field holds them. E = mc² counts that energy as mass. Only about 1 percent is the quarks themselves.
s.Heat {name} or run a current through it: Heat {name}, or run a current through it, and it glows in exactly these colors. They are the same everywhere in the universe. That is how we know what the stars are made of. Each line is one electron dropping between two levels. The photon carries away the difference. {LNOTE}
s.Helium's nucleus carries 2 positive char: Helium's nucleus carries 2 positive charges. Each electron feels a little less than both. The other electron spends part of its time between it and the nucleus. Slater's rules estimate what is left: the effective charge.
s.How the Sun begins. The weak force has t: This is how the Sun begins. The weak force has to turn a proton into a neutron in the middle of a collision. So a proton in the Sun's core waits billions of years, on average.
s.Hydrogen sits at the top of group 1 beca: Hydrogen sits at the top of group 1 because it has one outer electron, like {el}. But it is a nonmetal. It behaves very differently from the alkali metals.
s.Hydrogen, with one electron, is the one: Hydrogen has one electron. It is the one neutral atom solved exactly (step 5). Add a second electron and each one is pushed by the other as well as pulled by the nucleus. From there on, no exact formula exists. The standard shortcut:
s.In 1913 Niels Bohr simply declared it: t: In 1913 Niels Bohr simply declared it. The orbit's angular momentum must be a whole number times ℏ. An electron in an allowed orbit does not give off light. Light comes out only when it jumps down from one orbit to another. The rule is exact for one electron, so this step uses {ionWords}.
s.In Bohr's picture the innermost electron: In Bohr's picture the innermost electron moves at Z × α times the speed of light. Here α ≈ 1/137 is the fine-structure constant. For light atoms that is slow. For heavy atoms it is a large fraction of the speed of light. The electron gets heavier, its orbit pulls in, and the outer s orbits follow. That is why gold is yellow and mercury is a liquid. Slide Z to see where the simple formula breaks.
s.It sits right on the line where stable n: It sits right on the line where stable nuclei lie. But its neighbors with the same mass are held together more tightly. So it will turn into one of them by beta decay.
s.It snapped at {d} fm. The string held {Q: It snapped at {d} fm. The string held {Q} GeV. That is enough to make a {pair} quark and its antiquark out of the vacuum. The antiquark left with the quark you pulled ({meson}, {mesonQuarks}). The new quark took its place ({after}, {baryonQuarks}). Charge in, charge out: the same.
s.Keep falling, into {name}. Its atom is a: Keep falling, into {name}. Its atom is about {fmt} picometers across. Its nucleus is {fmt2} femtometers. That is {fmt3} times smaller. Make the nucleus a marble, and the atom would be {fmt4} meters wide. That is about {fields} football {fields, plural, one {field} other {fields}} end to end.
s.Keep falling, into {name}. Nobody has ma: Keep falling, into {name}. Nobody has made enough of it to measure how big its atom is. But its nucleus is about {fmt} femtometers across. The cloud around it is tens of thousands of times wider.
s.Keep pulling. Near 1.25 fm the string ho: Keep pulling. Near 1.25 fm the string holds about 1.1 GeV. That is more than it costs to make a quark and an antiquark out of the vacuum. So it snaps instead of stretching.
s.Learn it by doing it: build atoms and mo: Learn it by doing it. Build atoms and molecules. Explore the table's patterns. Work through the math of any atom. Test yourself. Run real experiments. Your progress stays in this browser.
s.Louis de Broglie's answer, in 1924: an e: Louis de Broglie's answer, in 1924: an electron is also a wave, with wavelength λ = h/p. A wave running around a loop only survives if it meets itself in step. So a whole number of wavelengths must fit around the orbit. That explains Bohr's rule. Slide the number of waves and watch what happens when it is not a whole number.
s.Mass rises with atomic number, with a fe: Mass rises with atomic number. There are a few famous swaps, where the table goes by protons, not mass. Argon is heavier than potassium. Cobalt is heavier than nickel. Tellurium is heavier than iodine.
s.Measured lines from the NIST Atomic Spec: These are measured lines from the NIST Atomic Spectra Database, converted from air to vacuum wavelengths. With more than one electron, the electrons push on each other. Then the Schrödinger equation has no exact solution. So these are measured, not computed.
s.Melting depends on bonding, not just on: Melting depends on bonding, not just on the atom. It peaks where atoms make the most bonds with each other: carbon in row 2, silicon in row 3, and vanadium, molybdenum, and tungsten among the metals. Then it drops away to the noble gases.
s.Mixing {pair} (one shell apart, one step: Mixing {pair} (one shell apart, one step of l apart), the cloud sloshes {sciT} times a second. That is exactly the frequency of the light this jump gives off: {nf} nm, {lightWord}.
s.Nitrogen has three bonds and one lone pa: Nitrogen has three bonds and one lone pair. Four groups make a tetrahedron again. But one corner holds only the lone pair. So the atoms form a short pyramid with nitrogen on top.
s.No nucleus with five particles holds tog: No nucleus with five particles holds together. None with eight lasts as long as a second. Those two gaps are a main reason the Big Bang made almost nothing heavier than lithium.
s.No quark ever comes out alone: the energ: No quark ever comes out alone. The energy you put in turns into new matter instead. That is confinement. Proving that the theory behind it has a mass gap is a million-dollar problem.
s.Nothing in this picture says which orbit: Nothing in this picture says which orbits are allowed. So it cannot explain why every {E} atom is the same size. The next step shows it is worse than that.
s.Nuclei are made of protons and neutrons: Nuclei are made of protons and neutrons packed together like drops of liquid. So the volume grows with the number of nucleons, A. The liquid-drop model counts the glue. Every nucleon bonds to its neighbors. The ones on the surface have fewer neighbors. The protons push each other apart. Nature prefers equal numbers of protons and neutrons, in pairs. The total is the binding energy. It is mass that disappeared when the nucleus formed: E = mc².
s.Nuclei this heavy decay by shedding an a: Nuclei this heavy decay by throwing off an alpha particle: two protons and two neutrons. That would make {lc}-{a}. One with extra neutrons may instead turn a neutron into a proton (beta-minus decay). Which wins depends on details this estimate cannot settle.
s.Nucleons fill shells, just like electron: Nucleons fill shells, just like electrons. Close a shell at 2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, or 126, and the nucleus is extra stable and round. Lead-208 is doubly magic. The thorium decay chain ends there. Three of the four decay chains end at lead: lead-206, lead-207, and lead-208.
s.On a shared computer, save your progress: On a shared computer, save your progress before you leave. Bring it back next time. A turn-in code is a one-line summary with no name on it. A teacher can read it in this same tab.
s.One mole of it, 6.022 × 10²³ units, weig: One mole of it is 6.022 × 10²³ units. It weighs {tot} grams. Each element's share of the mass is its atomic mass times how many of its atoms there are.
s.Open uranium's card and find it on the b: Open uranium's card and find it on the binding-energy curve. Past iron, each nucleon is held a little less tightly. So breaking a heavy nucleus in two releases energy.
s.Oxygen has four groups of electrons arou: Oxygen has four groups of electrons around it: two bonds and two lone pairs. They spread toward the corners of a tetrahedron. The lone pairs push a little harder. That closes the H–O–H angle from 109.5° to 104.5°. The two O–H pulls add up instead of canceling. So water has a negative end and a positive end. That is why it dissolves salt.
s.Per nucleon that binding peaks near iron: Per nucleon, that binding peaks near iron and nickel. Fusing light nuclei climbs the curve from one side. Splitting heavy ones climbs it from the other. That is the whole story of starlight and of reactors.
s.Photoelectron spectroscopy: X-rays knock: Photoelectron spectroscopy: X-rays knock electrons out of the atoms. Each electron leaves with the X-ray's energy minus the energy that held it. Count the electrons by that energy, and the shells appear as peaks. There is one peak per subshell. A peak is as tall as the number of electrons in it. It is farther left the more tightly they are held. This is how the shell structure of the table was confirmed. It is a core skill in AP Chemistry (Topic 1.6).
s.Pick an element and the tabs on the righ: Pick an element. The tabs on the right give its structure, its orbitals, its nucleus and isotopes, and where it is found and used. Open Math on any view to see exactly how each number was computed.
s.Pick technetium. It has no stable form a: Pick technetium. It has no stable form at all. Yet technetium-99m is used in about four out of five nuclear medicine scans. That is tens of millions a year.
s.Pick the elements and the kinds of quest: Pick the elements and the kinds of questions. Everyone who opens the link, or types the code, gets the same questions in the same order. Nothing is sent anywhere. The questions are rebuilt from the code itself.
s.Plot that per-nucleon binding against si: Plot that per-nucleon binding against size. It rises, peaks near iron, then falls. Below the peak, joining nuclei releases energy: fusion. Above it, splitting them does: fission. The Nucleus tab draws this curve with your nuclide marked.
s.Quark masses are the running masses from: The quark masses are the running masses from the Particle Data Group, about 2.2 and 4.7 MeV. They are only known to a few percent. The strong-force curve shows its shape and range, not a fitted strength.
s.Questions you miss come back after ten m: Questions you miss come back after ten minutes, then a day later. After that they come back less and less often, as long as you keep getting them right. Get three different questions right about one element, and you have mastered it.
s.Radiocarbon dating reaches back about 50: Radiocarbon dating reaches back about 50,000 years. After that, too little carbon-14 is left to count. For older rocks, geologists use slower clocks, such as uranium-238. Its half-life is 4.5 billion years.
s.Read the chance to tunnel. On top of tha: Read the chance to tunnel. On top of that, a proton must turn into a neutron by the weak force as they touch. So an average proton in the Sun's core waits billions of years. Fire once more.
s.Row lengths are 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32 &mda: The rows hold 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, and 32 elements. That is exactly the number of electrons each new set of orbitals can hold (2n², in the filling order). The table's odd shape is the quantum numbers made visible.
s.Set the electric pull equal to what a ci: Set the electric pull equal to what a circle needs, m v²/r, just as you would for a satellite. The answer is fast: thousands of kilometers a second. The electron goes around a few thousand trillion times a second.
s.Slater's estimate of the charge the oute: Slater's estimate of the charge the outermost electron feels. Across a row it climbs. Each new proton is only partly hidden by the electron added with it. Across the transition metals it climbs slowly, because the new d electrons hide more of it. This explains a lot about the shrinking radius and the rising electronegativity.
s.Slater's rules are a rule of thumb from: Slater's rules are a rule of thumb from 1930. This is where they break. For a p electron the estimate comes out three to five times too high. His rules give s and p electrons of the same shell one shielding value, as if a p electron were held as tightly as an s electron. For outer s electrons they do better. They land within about 20 percent for about half the elements, most of them heavy. For many light atoms and the first transition metals they are up to twice too high. Trends, under Explore, draws the estimate against the measured value for every element.

Slater's rules are a rule of thumb from 1930. For an outer s electron like this one, the estimate lands within about 20 percent for about half the elements, most of them heavy. For many light atoms and the first transition metals it is up to twice too high. For p electrons it does far worse. Modern calculations (Hartree–Fock and beyond) solve for all the electrons together. Trends, under Explore, draws the estimate against the measured value for every element.
s.Sound plays only when you press a button: Sound plays only when you press a button. Each line in an element's light becomes a tone exactly 40 octaves below the light itself. Redder light plays lower. Violet light plays higher. Every element has its own chord, with the light's real proportions.
s.Splitting one uranium-235 nucleus releas: Splitting one uranium-235 nucleus releases about 200 million electronvolts. That is millions of times more than burning one molecule of fuel. Reactors make nearly a tenth of the world's electricity this way.
s.Table salt is not made of molecules. Sod: Table salt is not made of molecules. Sodium gives its one outer electron to chlorine. The ions, Na⁺ and Cl⁻, stack in a cube. Each one is surrounded by six of the other. NaCl only says the ratio is one to one.
s.Ten steps from the outside of the atom i: Ten steps, from the outside of the atom in. Each question uses the step's equation and the numbers given. Work it on paper, then check it in Atom at {esc}.
s.That is enough to power a typical U.S. h: That is enough to power a typical U.S. home for {E} years. A home uses roughly 10,500 kWh of electricity a year. But only matter meeting antimatter turns all of its mass into energy.
s.That is {est} MeV per nucleon from the l: That is {est} MeV per nucleon from the liquid-drop formula. Building it released that energy. So the nucleus weighs {pct}% less than its loose parts: E = mc².
That is {est} MeV per nucleon from the liquid-drop formula. The measured value is {meas} MeV. Building it released that energy. So the nucleus weighs {pct}% less than its loose parts: E = mc².
s.The 4s electrons fill first but leave fi: The 4s electrons fill first, but they leave first. Once the 3d orbitals hold electrons, they sit lower in energy than 4s. They also shield the 4s from the nucleus. {sym}²⁺ is [Ar] 3d{sup}, with both 4s electrons gone.
s.The Big Bang should have made equal amou: The Big Bang should have made equal amounts of matter and antimatter. Antihydrogen falls down, not up (measured in 2023, to about 20%). The missing asymmetry is still missing.
s.The Coulomb-like term dominates up close: Up close, the Coulomb-like term is the biggest part. Far out, the linear σr term takes over. That is the tension of the flux tube, and it never lets go. Pull hard enough and the string snaps into new hadrons. It never frees a quark.
s.The app opens on the same table and goes: The app opens on the same table and goes deeper. It has every orbital of every element, the nuclear shell model, decay chains, and a guided tour. It is a single file of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It has no network access and no tracking. Run it on a Mac, on Windows, or on Linux, or open it in any modern browser. It is free and open source.
s.The blur on the stage is not a photograp: The blur on the stage is not a photograph and not a fog. It is a map of chance. It is bright where the electron is likely to be found, and dark where it almost never is. Drag to turn it.
s.The dark gaps are <b>nodes</b>, where th: The dark gaps are nodes. There the wave passes through zero, and the electron is never found. A {orb} orbital has {nr, plural, =0 {no spherical nodes} one {# spherical node} other {# spherical nodes}} and {l} through the middle. That is n − 1 = {all} in all.

The dark gaps are nodes. There the wave passes through zero, and the electron is never found. A {orb} orbital has {nr, plural, =0 {no spherical nodes} one {# spherical node} other {# spherical nodes}} and {l} through the middle. That is n − 1 = {all} in all. In a full subshell the flat ones cancel out. That is why it is round.
s.The dark gaps in an orbital are <b>nodes: The dark gaps in an orbital are nodes. There the wave passes through zero, and the electron is never found. The ground state has none. Here hydrogen is excited to 3p: one spherical node and one flat one. That is n − 1 = 2 in all.
s.The electron that puts it in the {blk} b: The electron that puts it in the {blk} block sits in a {orbName} orbital. That subshell is full, so it is perfectly round. The inner electrons shield it from the nucleus. So it feels a smaller charge (Slater’s rules, an estimate):
The electron that puts it in the {blk} block sits in a {orbName} orbital. The inner electrons shield it from the nucleus. So it feels a smaller charge (Slater’s rules, an estimate):
s.The energies are Slater’s estimates, the: The energies are Slater's estimates, the same rule of thumb the rest of Atom uses. So they are only roughly right. They are closest for the outermost s electrons. They are a fifth to a half too high for the 1s shell. They are two to five times too high for the other inner shells and for outer p electrons (Trends, under Explore, shows that gap). His rules also give the s and p electrons of one shell the same energy. So their two bars stand side by side here. In a measured spectrum they are two separate peaks, with the s peak to the left. Read the pattern: how many peaks, how tall, in what order.
The green line at 558 nm is the aurora. It is a 'forbidden' transition. It is so slow that only the thin upper air lets it shine.
s.The grid at the bottom is the periodic t: The grid at the bottom is the periodic table. Click any square and the whole model switches to that element: cloud, nucleus, and facts. The arrow keys step through the elements.
s.The page is lit by {el}’s own light, and: The page is lit by {el}’s own light. The rings around the atom are its lines, spread out by wavelength, the way a diffraction grating spreads them. Violet is nearest, red is farthest.
s.The string broke at {d} fm. The vacuum s: The string broke at {d} fm. The vacuum supplied {pair} and anti-{pair2}. The antiquark left with the quark you were holding ({meson} = {mesonQuarks}). The new quark took its place ({after} = {baryonQuarks}). Charge is conserved.
s.The strong force gets <em>weaker</em> at: The strong force gets weaker at short range. Probed at high energy, quarks rattle around almost freely. This is asymptotic freedom (2004 Nobel Prize). The Quarks tab plots how the strong coupling changes with energy.
s.The three valence quarks carry only part: The three valence quarks carry only part of the momentum. At Q²∼10 GeV² it is roughly gluons ~50%, valence ~36%, sea ~14% (the budget bar on the Quarks tab). The momentum adds up to 1:
s.This is hydrogen&rsquo;s one electron in: This is hydrogen's one electron in its ground state, 1s. It is computed, not drawn: ψ = R(r) · Y(θ, φ), a radial wave times a spherical one. The brightness is how likely you are to find the electron there. Hydrogen is the only atom whose equation can be solved exactly.
s.This is the crisis physicists faced arou: This is the crisis physicists faced around 1911, after Rutherford found the nucleus. Classical physics predicts collapse. Real atoms are stable. The rest of this tab is how that was fixed.
s.Those three are just the <em>valence</em: Those three are just the valence quarks. Around them boils a sea of virtual quark-antiquark pairs and gluons. At high energy, gluons carry about half the proton's momentum. See the momentum budget on the Quarks tab.
s.Three bonds and no lone pairs on boron:: Boron has three bonds and no lone pairs. The three groups lie flat, 120° apart, so the three pulls cancel. Boron has only six electrons around it, fewer than the usual eight. That makes BF₃ eager to take a pair from another molecule.
s.Turn the temperature to at least 10 keV,: Turn the temperature up to at least 10 keV, about 116 million kelvin, and fire again. Watch where the Gamow peak sits. Most reactions happen far below the barrier, by tunneling.
s.Two protons touching repel with about a: Two protons that touch push apart with about a million electron-volts. Something stronger, and very short-ranged, must hold them: the strong force. Yukawa's 1935 idea gives its range from the mass of the particle that carries it, the pion. Look deeper, and each proton and neutron is three quarks bound by gluons. Almost all of their mass is the energy of the quarks' motion and of the gluon field, not the quarks' own masses.
s.What each element is helping build right: What each element is helping build right now. Pick a field to light up its elements. Every card ends with an open problem that someone could take on.
s.What you have made your own. A ring mark: What you have made your own. A ring marks an element you have explored. A half-filled dot marks one you have built. A solid dot marks one you have mastered in the labs.
s.When the electron drops from level n₂ to: When the electron drops from level n₂ to n₁, the energy leaves as one photon. For a one-electron atom the arithmetic is exact. So this plot is computed, not looked up: 1/λ = RM Z² (1/n₁² − 1/n₂²). RM is the Rydberg constant, corrected for the recoil of the nucleus.{Z}
s.Where each element was made. Most of the: Where each element was made. Most of the hydrogen and helium are from the Big Bang. Everything heavier was made in stars, in their explosions, and in their collisions. Pick a source to see its share.
s.With this many neutrons the last one isn: With this many neutrons, the last one is not held at all. It leaves almost at once. Experiments find {iso} is the heaviest {el} that holds together. You have found the edge of the nuclear map.
With this many neutrons, the last one is not held at all. It would drip off almost at once. You have found the edge of the nuclear map. (Estimated from the liquid-drop model.)
s.Zoom past one proton or neutron and thre: Zoom past one proton or neutron and three little points appear in a churning field. Those points are quarks. As far as anyone can measure, they are truly pointlike. There are no smaller pieces inside.
s.{El} and {other} are in the same row, pe: {El} and {other} are in the same row, period {p}. So their outer electrons fill the same shell. Of the two, {right} is farther along, so it has more protons pulling on it.
s.{El} is {rows, plural, one {one row} oth: {El} is {rows, plural, one {one row} other {# rows}} lower. So its outer electrons are {rows, plural, one {a shell} other {# shells}} farther out. Even so, {el} holds its outer electron more tightly ({li} eV against {ui} eV). In heavy atoms the inner d and f electrons do not shield well. Relativity also pulls the outer electrons in.
s.{El}'s atom is about {ARAD} pm in radius: {El}'s atom is about {ARAD} pm in radius. Its nucleus is about {Rn} fm. That is {ratio} times smaller. Scale the nucleus up to a meter across, and the atom is {right} across. There is nothing but field in between. An atom is almost entirely empty.
s.{El}'s {z, plural, one {# electron} othe: {El}'s {z, plural, one {# electron} other {# electrons}} together weigh {me} u. That is {pct} percent of its {mA} u. The rest is in the nucleus. The nucleus is tens of thousands of times narrower than the atom.
s.{cap} is radioactive, but so slowly that: {cap} is radioactive, but very slowly. The {el} made before Earth formed is still here. Its half-life is about {pr} years, {ageCompare}. It decays by {PMODE}, becoming {pr2}.
s.{cap}'s nucleus carries {z} positive cha: {cap}'s nucleus carries {z} positive charges. But its outer electron does not feel all of them. The electrons in the inner shells sit in between and cancel part of the pull. Slater's rules estimate what is left: the effective charge.
s.{z} fill the orbitals in order (Pauli le: {z} fill the orbitals in order (Pauli lets two share each). Then let each electron feel the nucleus minus the electrons that shield it. Slater's rules put numbers on the shielding. Inner electrons hide almost all of a proton each. Electrons in the same shell hide only about a third.

atom.d: The smallest piece of an element that is still that element: a nucleus with electrons around it.

nucleus.d: The tiny, heavy center of an atom, made of protons and neutrons.

proton.d: A positive particle in the nucleus. The number of protons decides which element an atom is.

neutron.d: A particle in the nucleus with no charge. Neutrons help hold the nucleus together.

electron.d: A light, negative particle that lives in a cloud around the nucleus.

nucleon.d: A proton or a neutron: one of the particles that make up a nucleus.

quark.d: A tiny particle inside protons and neutrons. Each has three.

gluon.d: The particle that carries the strong force and holds quarks together.

strong force.d: The force that holds quarks inside protons and neutrons, and protons and neutrons inside a nucleus.

orbital.d: A region around the nucleus where an electron is likely to be found. It is a shape, not a path.

shell.d: A group of orbitals with about the same energy, numbered 1, 2, 3 ... from the nucleus outward.

subshell.d: Part of a shell: the s, p, d, or f orbitals of one shell.

configuration.d: A list of which orbitals an atom's electrons fill, such as 1s2 2s2 2p4.

valence.d: An electron in the outer shell. Valence electrons do the bonding.

ion.d: An atom that has lost or gained electrons, so it carries a charge.

cation.d: A positive ion: an atom that has lost electrons.

anion.d: A negative ion: an atom that has gained electrons.

isotope.d: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.

atomic number.d: The number of protons in a nucleus, written Z. It names the element.

mass number.d: The number of protons plus neutrons in a nucleus, written A.

atomic mass.d: The average mass of an element's atoms, in atomic mass units (u).

charge.d: The property that makes particles push or pull electrically. Protons are positive, electrons negative.

binding energy.d: The energy it would take to pull a nucleus apart into its protons and neutrons. It shows up as missing mass.

half-life.d: The time it takes for half of a radioactive sample to decay.

radioactive.d: Describes a nucleus that will break down on its own, giving off particles or energy.

decay.d: When an unstable nucleus changes into another nucleus, giving off a particle or energy.

alpha decay.d: A nucleus throws off a helium nucleus: two protons and two neutrons.

beta decay.d: A neutron turns into a proton (or the reverse), giving off an electron or positron.

fusion.d: Two light nuclei join into a heavier one, releasing energy. It powers the Sun.

fission.d: A heavy nucleus splits into two lighter ones, releasing energy. It powers reactors.

stable.d: A nucleus that does not decay. It stays the same forever, as far as we know.

photon.d: A particle of light. Its energy depends on its color (wavelength).

wavelength.d: The distance from one crest of a wave to the next. For light, it sets the color.

spectrum.d: Light spread out by wavelength, like a rainbow, showing which colors are present.

spectral line.d: One sharp color an element gives off or absorbs. Each element has its own set.

energy level.d: One of the allowed energies an electron can have in an atom.

ground state.d: The lowest-energy arrangement of an atom's electrons.

excited state.d: An atom whose electron has jumped to a higher energy level.

ionization energy.d: The energy needed to pull one electron off an atom.

electronegativity.d: How strongly an atom pulls shared electrons toward itself in a bond.

atomic radius.d: How big an atom is, measured from the nucleus to the outer edge of its electron cloud.

period.d: A row of the periodic table. Elements in a row have the same number of shells.

group.d: A column of the periodic table. Elements in a column behave alike.

block.d: A region of the table named for the subshell being filled: s, p, d, or f.

noble gas.d: An element in the last column, with a full outer shell. They hardly react.

alkali metal.d: A metal in the first column, from lithium down (not hydrogen). They have one outer electron and react violently with water.

halogen.d: An element in the second-to-last column. They need one more electron and react strongly.

transition metal.d: A metal in the middle of the table, filling a d subshell.

lanthanide.d: One of the fifteen elements from lanthanum to lutetium, filling the 4f subshell.

density.d: How much mass fits in a given space: grams per cubic centimeter.

melting point.d: The temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid.

boiling point.d: The temperature at which a liquid turns into a gas.

mole.d: A counting unit: 6.022 × 10²³ atoms or molecules.

molar mass.d: The mass of one mole of a substance, in grams.

molecule.d: Two or more atoms joined by bonds, such as H₂O.

bond.d: A link between atoms made by sharing or giving electrons.

covalent bond.d: A bond where two atoms share a pair of electrons.

ionic bond.d: A bond where one atom gives electrons to another, and the ions attract.

lone pair.d: A pair of outer electrons on an atom that is not used in a bond.

polar.d: A molecule with a positive end and a negative end, because electrons are shared unevenly.

shielding.d: Inner electrons blocking part of the nucleus's pull on the outer electrons.

effective charge.d: The pull an outer electron really feels: the nucleus's charge minus the shielding.

probability.d: How likely something is. An orbital is a map of probability.

wave function.d: The mathematical wave that describes an electron. Its square gives the probability.

node.d: A place in an orbital where the wave is zero, so the electron is never found.

quantum number.d: A whole number that labels an electron's orbital: n for size, l for shape, m for direction.

Coulomb's law.d: The rule for electric force: stronger for bigger charges, weaker with distance squared.

Bohr model.d: The 1913 picture of electrons on fixed orbits. It gives the right energies for atoms with one electron, such as hydrogen, and fails for all the others.

relativity.d: Einstein's physics for things moving near the speed of light. It matters for heavy atoms.

E = mc².d: Energy equals mass times the speed of light squared: mass and energy are the same thing.

magic number.d: A number of protons or neutrons (2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126) that makes a nucleus extra stable.

liquid-drop model.d: A way to estimate binding energy by treating the nucleus like a drop of liquid.

valley of stability.d: The band of proton and neutron counts where nuclei are stable.

tunneling.d: A quantum trick: a particle gets through a barrier it does not have the energy to climb.

Coulomb barrier.d: The electric push two nuclei must overcome to get close enough to fuse.

plasma.d: A gas so hot that its atoms have lost their electrons.

photoelectron spectroscopy.d: An experiment that knocks electrons out of atoms with X-rays and measures how tightly each was held.

confinement.d: The rule that quarks can never be pulled out alone. The energy makes new particles instead.

antimatter.d: Matter's mirror twin. When matter meets antimatter, both turn into energy.

meson.d: A particle made of one quark and one antiquark.

baryon.d: A particle made of three quarks, such as a proton or a neutron.

pion.d: The lightest meson. Its mass sets the range of the strong force.

femtometer.d: A millionth of a billionth of a meter (10⁻¹⁵ m), the size of a nucleus.

picometer.d: A trillionth of a meter (10⁻¹² m). Atoms are a few hundred picometers across.

nanometer.d: A billionth of a meter (10⁻⁹ m). Visible light has wavelengths of about 380 to 750 nm.

electronvolt.d: A small unit of energy: what one electron gains crossing one volt. MeV is a million of them.

kelvin.d: The temperature scale that starts at absolute zero. 0 °C is 273.15 K.

frequency.d: How many waves pass per second. Higher frequency means more energy.

Rydberg formula.d: The formula that gives every spectral line of hydrogen from two whole numbers.

Schrödinger equation.d: The equation of quantum mechanics that gives the wave function of an electron.

Pauli exclusion principle.d: No two electrons in an atom can be in exactly the same state: at most two per orbital, with opposite spins.

Hund's rule.d: Electrons spread out across the orbitals of a subshell before any orbital gets a second one.

Aufbau principle.d: Electrons fill the lowest-energy orbitals first.

spin.d: A built-in property of particles, like a tiny magnet. Electrons come in two spins: up and down.

supernova.d: The explosion of a dying star. It makes and scatters many heavy elements.

neutron star.d: The collapsed core of a dead star, made almost entirely of neutrons. Two merging make gold.

Big Bang.d: The beginning of the universe, about 13.8 billion years ago. It made the hydrogen and helium.

cosmic ray.d: A fast particle from space. Cosmic rays make lithium, beryllium, boron, and carbon-14.

abundance.d: How common an element is, for example in Earth's crust.

crust.d: Earth's thin outer rock layer, the part we live on and mine.

semiconductor.d: A material, like silicon, that conducts only when told to. Chips are made of it.

superconductor.d: A material that carries electricity with no resistance at all when it is cold enough.

catalyst.d: A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up.

alloy.d: A metal mixed with other elements, such as steel (iron with carbon).

oxide.d: A compound of an element with oxygen, such as rust (iron oxide).

acid.d: A substance that gives away hydrogen ions in water. Sour, and it reacts with metals.

tetrahedron.d: A shape with four triangular faces. Methane's four bonds point to its corners.

vacuum.d: Space with nothing in it. In quantum physics, even that seethes with short-lived particles.

Monte Carlo.d: A way to draw a picture from chance: throw random points and keep the ones the odds allow.
